entities.name: Harper's Bazaar
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Harper's Bazaar, founded on November 2, 1867, in New York City, stands as a pivotal institution in the realm of fashion journalism and cultural commentary. As one of the first American women's magazines, it has played a crucial role in shaping women's fashion and societal norms over more than a century. Originally published as a weekly by Harper & Brothers, it transitioned to a monthly format and was acquired by Hearst Communications in 1913, further solidifying its influence within the industry.

The magazine has been a platform for both emerging and established designers, showcasing trends and innovations in fashion. Throughout its history, it has featured iconic photographers and writers, including Richard Avedon and Diana Vreeland, who have contributed to its reputation for high-quality visual storytelling and editorial content. Harper's Bazaar has chronicled the evolution of fashion through significant historical events, such as the flapper movement in the 1920s and the rise of feminist fashion in the 1960s, reflecting and influencing societal changes.

The legacy of Harper's Bazaar extends beyond fashion; it has contributed to the discourse on women's roles in society, challenging norms and encouraging empowerment through style. The magazine's commitment to beauty and aesthetics has made it a cultural touchstone, influencing not only fashion but also advertising and media practices. Its ongoing presence in the digital age, with a robust online platform, ensures that its legacy continues to evolve and resonate with new generations.

As noted by fashion historian Valerie Steele, 'Harper's Bazaar has been a vital force in defining American fashion and its cultural implications, serving as a mirror to the evolving identity of women in society.'
